The bug report targets GCC's internal overflow-rewriting logic, specifically rewrite_to_defined_overflow / gimple_with_undefined_signed_overflow. This logic is used when GCC wants to preserve or model wrapping behavior explicitly instead of leaving signed overflow as undefined behavior during optimization.

The missing case is a VCE, i.e. a GIMPLE value-conversion expression, when the conversion is between integral types. In this context, the report says such conversions should be rewritten into explicit casts as part of the overflow-rewrite process.

The issue matters because some optimizers and statement-moving passes treat ordinary arithmetic with undefined signed overflow differently from operations rewritten into defined forms. If integral VCEs are not rewritten consistently, later passes may reason about the converted value under the wrong overflow assumptions.

The report explicitly references phiopt's move_stmt as already implementing the desired handling. That indicates there is existing GCC code showing the intended model: when moving or rewriting statements, integral conversions that can participate in signed-overflow-sensitive reasoning are converted into plain casts so their semantics remain valid after the transformation.

The likely failure mode is not a wrong front-end parse or code-generation crash, but an internal mismatch in optimizer semantics: one path rewrites arithmetic to defined-overflow form, but leaves integral conversion expressions untouched, causing inconsistent GIMPLE after transformation.

Conversions between integral types can affect whether a value is viewed as sign-extending, truncating, or changing precision. In overflow-sensitive transformations, that matters because narrowing and widening conversions are part of the effective arithmetic semantics, especially when signed values are involved.

If such a VCE remains in a form still associated with undefined signed-overflow reasoning, subsequent optimization may incorrectly fold, hoist, merge, or compare expressions on the assumption that signed overflow cannot happen, even though the rewrite pass intended to make the behavior explicit and defined.

The mention of 'from/to integral types' narrows the bug scope: the requested rewrite applies when both source and destination are integer-like scalar types. The report does not claim the same need for floating-point, pointer, or non-integral conversions.

Because the reproducer content is absent, the concrete observable symptom could have been a miscompile, a failed compiler self-check, or a mismatch in tree/GIMPLE dumps. But from the report text alone, the essential exercised behavior is: GCC processes a GIMPLE statement containing an integral value conversion in a context where undefined signed overflow is being rewritten, and it currently fails to canonicalize that conversion into a cast.

The requested fix implies the correct compiler behavior is to treat these integral VCEs as semantic casts during rewriting, so all pieces of the transformed expression consistently obey defined-overflow semantics and later passes see the intended canonical form.

gcc/tree-ssa-phiopt.cc.summary: Given a "diamond" control-flow pattern where BB0 tests a condition, BB1 and BB2 are "then" and "else" blocks dependent on this test, and BB3 rejoins control flow following BB1 and BB2, look for opportunities to hoist loads as follows. If BB3 contains a PHI of two loads, one each occurring in BB1 and BB2, and the loads are provably of adjacent fields in the same structure, then move both loads into BB0. Of course this can only be done if there are no dependencies preventing such motion. One of the hoisted loads will always be speculative, so the transformation is currently conservative: - The fields must be strictly adjacent. - The two fields must occupy a single memory block that is guaranteed to not cross a page boundary. The last is difficult to prove, as such memory blocks should be aligned on the minimum of the stack alignment boundary and the alignment guaranteed by heap allocation interfaces. Thus we rely on a parameter for the alignment value. Provided a good value is used for the last case, the first restriction could possibly be relaxed.

Those methods have both STATIC and EXTERNAL set. 2) In WHOPR mode devirtualization might lead to reference to method that was partitioned elsehwere. In this case we have static VAR_DECL or FUNCTION_DECL that has no corresponding callgraph/varpool node declaring the body. 3) COMDAT functions referred by external vtables that we devirtualize only during final compilation stage. At this time we already decided that we will not output the function body and thus we can't reference the symbol directly.

This function implicitly defines the middle-end type system. With the notion of 'a < b' meaning that useless_type_conversion_p (a, b) holds and 'a > b' meaning that useless_type_conversion_p (b, a) holds, the following invariants shall be fulfilled: 1) useless_type_conversion_p is transitive. reviewed_methods.summary: Return true if the conversion from INNER_TYPE to OUTER_TYPE is a useless type conversion, otherwise return false. This function implicitly defines the middle-end type system. With the notion of 'a < b' meaning that useless_type_conversion_p (a, b) holds and 'a > b' meaning that useless_type_conversion_p (b, a) holds, the following invariants shall be fulfilled: 1) useless_type_conversion_p is transitive. If a < b and b < c then a < c. 2) useless_type_conversion_p is not symmetric. From a < b does not follow a > b. 3) Types define the available set of operations applicable to values. A type conversion is useless if the operations for the target type is a subset of the operations for the source type. For example casts to void* are useless, casts from void* are not (void* can't be dereferenced or offsetted, but copied, hence its set of operations is a strict subset of that of all other data pointer types). Casts to const T* are useless (can't be written to), casts from const T* to T* are not.
